title: Submicrowatt-driven near-infrared luminescence from perovskite-fluoride quantum-cutting heterostructures for gas sensing

paper_content.abstract: The pursuit of wideband tunable near-infrared (NIR) light sources has reached fever pitch due to advances in photonic chips, optical communications, and molecular trace detection. Lanthanide ions (Ln3+), renowned for their characteristic NIR luminescence, have nevertheless been stymied by the challenges of an extremely low molar extinction coefficient and linear absorption. Herein, a sensitisation methodology is presented that capitalises on the quantum cutting-engineered heterostructure nanoparticles (CsPbX : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+), to achieve multi-wavelength 3 4 NIR luminescence spanning the 900-2200 nm spectrum. The designed heterostructure exhibits an unprecedented absorption bandwidth (200–690 nm) across the UV-visible spectrum, with an exceptionally low stimulation threshold at the sub-microwatt level (50 µW cm-2). The NIR luminescent wavelengths can be precisely modulate by meticulously adjusting the dopant Ln3+ ions leveraging Yb3+-mediated quantum cutting processes. Spectroscopic analysis reveals a directed energy transfer pathway at the perovskite-fluoride heterogeneous interface: perovskite host→Yb3+ (perovskite) →Yb3+ (NaYF4) →Ln3+. This architecture demonstrates multiplexed gas detection capabilities under AI-assisted analysis, facilitating the simultaneous identification and monitoring of multiple marker gases in complex environments. Our work provides a scalable strategy for constructing ultra-broadband NIR light sources, with implications for high-throughput spectroscopic sensing.
paper_content.introduction:
Near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy holds a great promise as a sensing technique because it provides rich fingerprint information that accurately identifies numerous gases through their specific absorption wavelengths1-7. Nevertheless, most current near-infrared gas sensing systems rely on on-chip techniques that employ costly single-wavelength infrared lasers. The operational wavelength range of on-chip sensors is inherently defined by the single-mode and optical guiding conditions of the waveguides. This consequently restricts the detection to specific gases, significantly limiting sensor selectivity8-10. Consequently, developing broadband near-infrared light sources with wide wavelength coverage and scalable manufacturing capabilities is crucial for overcoming this technological bottleneck. In contrast to costly and complex-to-prepare traditional infrared-emitting semiconductors like GaAs11, 12, InP13, 14, and PbS15, 16, lanthanide ions (Ln3+) doped nanomaterials offer numerous advantages, including abundant infrared emitting energy levels, diverse spectral emission bands, large Stokes shifts, and stable photochemistry17-22. This makes them a promising choice for constructing high-quality NIR light sources.

Considerable progress has been made in recent years in research on rare-earth-activated NIR luminescence. However, two critical challenges impede its application in infrared gas detection: (1) The emission of existing NIR luminescent materials is predominantly limited to narrow, isolated bands, such as Er3+ at 1530 nm23, Tm3+ at 808 nm24, Nd3+ at 1064 nm25, Tm3+ at 1460 nm26, and Ho3+ at 2000 nm27. This constraint substantially restricts the variety and range of detectable gases and hinders the selective development of infrared gas detection technologies for multiple marker gases. (2) The intrinsic parity-forbidden nature of 4f–4f electronic transitions in Ln3+ ions results in an extremely low molar extinction coefficient (typically <10 cm-1·M-1) and linear absorption behavior confined to discrete laser wavelengths (e.g., 808 nm, 980 nm, and 1540 nm)18-20, 28. Consequently, exciting rare-earth ions for NIR emission requires the use of multiple lasers with specific wavelengths that match the energy levels of different ions. To advance the development of multiplexed and selective NIR gas sensors, both issues must be addressed at the level of light source design. Recent efforts have explored various strategies to mitigate these limitations, such as employing Cr3+ sensitization to reduce the excitation threshold for NIR emission29, and utilizing symmetric core–shell nanostructures to achieve broadband excitation via co-sensitization of Ho3+ and Nd3+ 30. Although these strategies have yielded notable advancements, they have not yet addressed the fundamental limitations of rare-earth-based NIR luminescence, namely its narrow emission spectrum and dependence on discrete excitation wavelengths. Therefore, it is challenging to build the efficient multi-wavelength NIR light sources with low excitation thresholds and broad excitation bands.

Lead halide perovskite quantum dots (PeQDs) possess a significant absorption cross-section, provide broad and adjustable UV-visible absorption, and can be excited within an extensive range from 200 to 700 nm31-33. Their perfect octahedral coordination makes them a promising host material for lanthanide ions34. Particularly, Yb3+ ion doped PeQDs demonstrated the efficient quantum cutting behavior, extending the emission wavelength to the NIR range35, 36. However, a valence mismatch between Ln3+ and Pb 2+ ions imposes restrictions on the Ln3+ doping concentration in PeQDs, significantly hindering the achievement of efficient multi-wavelength NIR luminescence. As reported by Zhang and colleagues, PeQDs can effectively unite with NaYF , 4 which serves as an exceptional host for Ln3+ ions37, 38. Consequently, we formulated a bold hypothesis: could we develop a low-power excitation source for efficient NIR light emission by employing Yb3+ ion doped PeQDs to enhance the absorption cross-section, doping a high concentration of Ln3+ ions into the NaYF host, and effectively merging them through a core-shell 4 heterostructure structure? Importantly, the well-established nanocrystal core-shell coating technique using NaYF can seamlessly incorporate various Ln3+ ions into a cohesive system30, 39, 4 40, thus establishing a promising foundation for implementing NIR spectrum gas detection technology with comprehensive wavelength coverage.

Building upon the considerations above, we present an innovative sensitization approach to achieve ultra-wideband excitation and finely tuned NIR luminescence using heterostructure nanoparticles denoted as CsPbX : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ (Fig.1). Our sensitization strategy 3 4 employed PeQDs as the optical absorption antennae, Yb3+ ions doped in both PeQDs and NaYF 4 as the collaborative energy transfer medium, and Ln3+ ions as the activators responsible for generating NIR luminescence. This approach involves creating a energy transfer pathway from the perovskite host to Yb3+ ions in the perovskite host, then to Yb3+ ions in NaYF shell and finally to 4 the Ln3+ ions, referred to as PeQD-Yb3+ (PeQD)-Yb3+ (NaYF ) -Ln3+. The process begins with the 4 absorption of incident photons by the PeQD. Electrons on the conduction band of the PeQD are then transferred to Yb3+ ions via a quantum cutting process. Subsequently, energy is transferred to the luminescent Ln3+ through interfacial energy transfer between Yb3+ ions in the PeQDs and Yb3+ ions in the NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+, ultimately leading to multi-wavelength near-infrared luminescence. 4 The PeQDs provide NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ with ultra-wideband absorption capabilities, while the joint 4 medium Yb3+ ion facilitates excitation energy transfer to each luminescent Ln3+ ion. Unlike prior nanoparticles doped with Ln3+ ion that achieved NIR emission, the heterostructure, sensitized by PeQDs, exhibits a wide excitation band spanning from 200 to 690 nm. Therefore, this proposed sensitization strategy enables the efficient acquisition of NIR fluorescence with a broad response across the UV-visible spectrum compliance to various excitation requirements, including low-power white light and multi-wavelength excitation, as opposed to a limited selection of single wavelength lasers. Furthermore, we have successfully integrated NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+, and PeQDs 4 doped with diverse luminescence centers into a unified multilayer core–shell nanoparticles. This multilayer core–shell nanoparticles can dedicate multi-wavelength fluorescence within the 900-2200 nm range under low-power white-light excitation conditions, demonstrating significant potential for multiplexed gas detection applications.

Fig.1 illustrates the mechanism underlying the high-efficiency generation of NIR emissions. Upon the combination of CsPbX : Yb3+ and NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ (Ln=Ho, Er, Tm, Ce), the CsPbX 3 4 3 PeQDs demonstrate broad excitation coverage in the UV-visible spectrum, and NaYF provides 4 an ample supply of sites for doping Ln3+ ions. Directly energy transfer through the joint mediator Yb3+ ions significantly enhances the electron population within the E energy level of Ln3+ ions. 2 This enhancement leads to a substantial improvement in the NIR emission. The outermost layer of NaYF effectively mitigates energy losses caused by surface defects41. Notably, the efficient 4 quantum cutting process, exhibiting a photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of ~148.4%, amplifies the energy transfer mechanism, continuously enhancing NIR fluorescence emissions (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). During the initial phase of the experiment, we adjusted the NIR fluorescence characteristics of Ln3+ ions doped NaYF by precisely changing the 4 concentration of dopant ions. It is well known that Ln3+ ions like Ho3+, Er3+, Tm3+ have the ability to emit at NIR region. Four kinds of nanoparticles (NPs) (NaYF : Yb3+, Tm3+@ NaYF , NaYF : 4 4 4 Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+@ NaYF , NaYF : Yb3+, Ho3+@ NaYF , NaYF : Yb3+, Ho3+, Ce3+@ NaYF ) were 4 4 4 4 4 synthesized using a standard solvothermal method42. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image analysis displays uniform spherical NPs with an average diameter of approximately 35 nm (Supplementary Fig. 2). The presence of well-defined lattice stripes with a spacing of 0.52 nm indicates the high crystallinity of the as-prepared NPs. The hexagonal phase structure of the NPs was confirmed by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) measurement (Supplementary Fig. 3). Elemental mapping images (Supplementary Fig. 4) further elucidate the spatial distribution of elements within the core-shell structure. The emission spectra of Tm/Yb, Er/Yb/Ce, Ho/Yb, and Ho/Yb/Ce doped NaYF are shown in Fig. 2a, pumped by a 980 nm light source. Tm3+, Er3+, and 4 Ho3+ ions contribute to NIR emission at wavelengths of 1460 nm (3H -3F ), 1527 nm (4I -4I ), 4 4 13/2 15/2 1180 nm (5I -5I ), and 1952 nm (5I -5I ), with their respective energy level transitions outlined in 6 8 7 8 Fig. 2d. Particularly, the introduction of Ce3+ ions produces an effective cross-relaxation pathway for Ce3+-Er3+ (4I +2F →4I +2F ) and Ce3+-Ho3+ (5I +2F →5I +2F ) ion pairs, hence 11/2 5/2 13/2 7/2 6 5/2 7 7/2 generating the NIR strong emissions of Er3+ ions at 1527 nm and Ho3+ ions at 1952 nm43, 44. Fig. 2b-2c and Supplementary Fig. 5-8 show the strong correlations between NIR fluorescence intensity and dopant ion concentrations. The ideal doping concentration for Tm3+ ions is only 0.6% due to significant concentration quenching effect, whereas Er3+ and Ho3+ ions have optimal concentrations of 5% and 6%, respectively. Doping with 6% Ho3+ ions is necessary to obtain the maximum luminescence at both 1180 nm and 1952 nm. Interestingly, doping with Ce3+ ions enhances the 1952 nm emission of Ho3+ ions, but at the expense of the 1180 nm emission intensity (Fig. 2b and Fig. 2d). This phenomenon can be attributed to the cross-relaxation process 5I +2F →5I +2F , which accelerates the transition of electrons from the 5I energy level to the 6 5/2 7 7/2 6 5I energy level, leading to a significant increase in the electron population at the 5I energy level 7 7 (Fig. 2d). As a result, the emission at 1180 nm decreases while the emission at 1952 nm increases. Following rigorous modulation of dopant ion concentrations, the optimal NIR nanoparticles were ultimately synthesized: NaYF : 0.6% Tm3+, 25% Yb3+@ NaYF ; NaYF : 5% Er3+, 35% Yb3+, 4% 4 4 4 Ce3+@ NaYF ; NaYF : 6% Ho3+, 20% Yb3+@ NaYF ; and NaYF : 6% Ho3+, 20% Yb3+, 6% Ce3+@ 4 4 4 4 NaYF , respectively. 4

In order to produce the previous mentioned multi-band emissions in a single NP, it is feasible to create a multilayer core-shell NPs with several emitting centers. Based on the penetration depth of NIR light, the multilayer core-shell structure was constructed. The core, NaYF : 6% Ho3+, 20% 4 Yb3+, 6% Ce3+, exhibited emissions centered at 1180 nm and 1952 nm. Multilayer core-shell nanoparticles (NaYF : 6%Ho3+, 20%Yb3+, 6%Ce3+@NaYF : 5%Er3+, 35%Yb3+, 4%Ce3+@NaYF : 4 4 4 0.6%Tm3+, 25%Yb3+@NaYF ), short for CSSS, were created by a sequential coating technique. 4 Morphological and structural analysis of CSSS, illustration in Supplementary Fig. 9-11, confirmed a homogeneous hexagonal-phase multilayered core-shell structure. Notably, the multi-band NIR emission spectra of CSSS is depicted in Fig. 2e and achieves 1180 nm, 1460 nm, 1527 nm and 1952 nm emissions within a single NP. The core-shell design enables the multi-band NIR emissions, but the absorption and excitation problems remain to be solved before practical applications, and we are all well-aware of the narrow-band absorption problem caused by the 4f forbidden transition of rare-earth ions.

For an advanced NIR light source, a wide range of absorption and excitation is needed to adapt to a variety of operating conditions, such as the uncertain excitation wavelength and power. To overcome the inherent constraint posed by the limited absorption cross-section of Ln3+ ions and obtain a highly efficient NIR light source, we create a heterostructure through combining the PeQDs with NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ NPs, specifically Yb3+ doped PeQDs embedded in a matrix of 4 NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ NPs with a NaYF passivation shell, denoted as PeQD -NPs (CsPbX : Yb3+- 4 4 Yb Ln 3 NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+@NaYF (X=Cl, Br, I; Ln = Ho, Er, Tm, Ce)), as shown in Fig. 3a. In this 4 4 structure, PeQDs with a wide absorption band ranging serves as the light absorber, which can sensitize the emitters in the NaYF matrix through energy transfer process. Notably, a distinctive 4 aspect of our methodology involves the use of oleylamine bromide (OAmBr) as a stabilizing agent for the PeQDs structure, as detailed in the Supplementary Information.45, 46 Since the inert NaYF 4 coating can obscure the resolution of the PeQD, characterization was performed on uncoated CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ heterostructure (Supplementary Fig. 12-13). The 1.5 1.5 4 addition of an outer undoped NaYF shell was a subsequent optimization step to enhance material 4 stability and luminescence efficiency. The high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) image measurement of CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Er3+, Ce3+ heterostructure was performed in order to clearly distinguish the creation of the heterostructure (Fig. 3b-d). Based on their bright and dark fluctuations, it is evident that the PeQDs (dark area) are uniformly distributed in NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+. The heterostructure NPs 4 (CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+) have an average total size of about 27.3 nm 1.5 1.5 4 (Supplementary Fig. 12). After coating with an inert NaYF shell (3.91 nm thick), the final size of 4 the NPs increases to about 35.1 nm (Supplementary Fig. 13). The magnified image of Fig. 3c shows that the PeQDs have different shapes and variable sizes, which can be attributed to the dissolution phenomenon during the formation of the heterostructure37, 47. The high-resolution energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) mapping images clearly illustrate the spatial distribution of Er and Yb, revealing that Er is predominantly localized at the outer region of the heterostructure, whereas Yb exhibits a homogeneous distribution throughout the entire heterostructure matrix (Fig. 3d), which indicates that the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+ PeQDs are 1.5 1.5 successfully ensembled in NaYF :Ln matrix. Furthermore, high-resolution transmission electron 4 microscopy (HRTEM) imaging, performed with a spherical aberration corrector, directly reveals the lattice fringes of the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+ and NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+, allowing for the 1.5 1.5 4 determination of their relative orientations (Fig. 3e). The heterogeneous interface of CsPbCl Br : 1.5 1.5 Yb3+ and NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ can be clearly distinguished. The in-situ mapping results further 4 reveal the distribution of Yb in the two different lattice environments (Fig. 3f). Moreover, the general level EDS also clearly shows the distribution of the elements, providing evidence for the formation of the heterostructure (Fig. 3g). Line scan analyses at the atomic level consistently reveal the distribution of elements (especially Pb, which are clustered only in the core) as well as the heterostructure boundaries, which provide sufficient evidence for the formation of CsPbCl Br : 1.5 1.5 Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ heterostructure (Fig. 3h). Similarly, PeQD -NPs , PeQD -NPs , 4 Yb Yb/Tm Yb Yb/Ho and PeQD -NPs have also been characterised and all exhibit well-defined heterostructure Yb Yb/Ho/Ce (Supplementary Fig. 12-16). The XRD results jointly confirm the superior crystalline quality of the heterostructure nanoparticles, showing only the PeQD and NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+ phases with 4 no additional phases detected (Supplementary Fig. 17). Furthermore, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was employed for compositional analysis of the films consisting of CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce 3+, at varying etching depths (Supplementary Fig. 18). 1.5 1.5 4 When etching depth up to 3 nm, there is a rapid reduction in the elemental content of Y, Yb, Er, and Ce. Conversely, the proportions of Pb and Cl slightly increased (Fig. 3i). The evidence presented above conclusively affirms the successful synthesis of the heterostructure in PeQD - Yb NPs Ln .

Spectroscopic characterisation was carried out to characterise the optical properties of the PeQD -NPs heterostructure. The PeQD -NPs , CsPbX : Yb3+-NaYF : 35%Yb3+, 5%Er3+, Yb Ln Yb Yb/Er/Ce 3 4 4%Ce3+@NaYF (X=Cl, Br, I), typically exhibits tunable broadband absorption, as illustrated in 4 Supplementary Fig. 19. The excitation spectra monitored at 1527 nm can be effectively modulated by adjusting the composition of the PeQDs, enabling optimal coverage of the ultra-wide range from 200-690 nm (Supplementary Fig. 20). As shown in Fig. 4a, PeQD -NPs exhibits a Yb Yb/Er/Ce remarkable excitation advantage compared to the narrow excitation linewidth of Ln3+ ions in NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+@NaYF . This advantage is characterised by a significant broaden of the 4 4 excitation wavelength and a remarkable increase in the intensity of the excitation spectra. A consistent agreement is observed across datasets PeQD -NPs , PeQD -NPs , and Yb Yb/Tm Yb Yb/Ho PeQD -NPs (Supplementary Fig. 21). These findings suggest that the heterostructure of Yb Yb/Ho/Ce PeQD -NPs plays a crucial role in reducing the excitation threshold for the NIR emission of Yb Ln NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+, and indicate that the PeQD -NPs system holds significant potential for 4 Yb Ln achieving efficient NIR luminescence with broadband, low-threshold excitation. Amazingly, PeQD -NPs can be independently pumped by multiple wavelengths, enabling the Yb Yb/Er/Ce collection of robust NIR luminescence under white-light irradiation, as shown in Fig. 4b. This marks a significant achievement in producing NIR emission under white light illumination.

Importantly, according to the power-dependent spectrum, the excitation power threshold for PeQD -NPs at 1527 nm is approximately 50 µW cm⁻², which is 306 times lower than that Yb Yb/Er/Ce of NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+@NaYF (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 22). At the excitation power 4 4 threshold (15.3 mW cm-2) of NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+@NaYF , the emission intensity of PeQD - 4 4 Yb NPs is nearly 80 times higher than that of NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+@NaYF (Fig. 4c). Fig. Yb/Er/Ce 4 4 4d and Supplementary Fig. 23 show the intensity of the NIR spectrum as the halide composition of PeQDs changes. Notably, the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NPs exhibit the highest NIR luminescence 1.5 1.5 Ln intensity. CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NPs displayed an intensity 96.1 times greater than that of 1.5 1.5 Yb/Er/Ce NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+@NaYF . A significant reduction in NIR luminescence is observed as the 4 4 halogen ions transform to Br and I. This phenomenon is attributed to the alteration of PeQDs bandgap, disrupting the requisite conditions for Yb3+ ions to achieve quantum cutting. To further evaluate the NIR emission performance of PeQD -NPs , the PLQY of CsPbCl Br : Yb3+- Yb Ln 1.5 1.5 NPs was measured at 1527 nm, reaching approximately 23.45%. This value significantly Er/Yb/Ce surpasses that of the infrared-emitting fluorescent materials currently reported (see Supplementary Table 2). Similarly, PeQD -NPs , PeQD -NPs , and PeQD -NPs can also Yb Yb/Tm Yb Yb/Ho Yb Yb/Ho/Ce generate NIR emission through the same mechanism as PeQD -NPs , producing NIR Yb Yb/Er/Ce fluorescence at multiple distinct wavelengths (Fig. 4e). Furthermore, we designed and synthesized the heterostructure NPs with four coating shells, CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : 6% Ho3+, 20% Yb3+, 1.5 1.5 4 6% Ce3+@NaYF : 5% Er3+, 35% Yb3+, 4% Ce3+@NaYF : 0.6% Tm3+, 25% Yb3+@NaYF , short 4 4 4 for PeQD -CSSS. The morphological evolution at each stage of the preparation process is Yb illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 24, revealing that the final composite structure exhibits a NP size of approximately 47.8 nm. Under white light excitation, the PeQD -CSSS emits multiple NIR Yb wavelengths spanning from 900 to 2200 nm, as demonstrated in Fig. 4f. The PLQY measured for the photoluminescence in the 900–1700 nm range is approximately 37.1%. The ultra-wide NIR emission, broad absorption band and low excitation threshold enable the NIR light source to perform a range of infrared spectroscopy applications.

This tunable multi-wavelength light source, when integrated with NIR spectroscopy for gas detection applications, such as replacing existing chromatograph light sources, will play a pivotal role in deciphering gas molecules within enigmatic environments, holding potential for remote detection of exoplanetary atmospheres. This technological synergy facilitates not only the meticulous analysis of atmospheric gas compositions but also the identification of latent biosignatures, thereby paving the way for a comprehensive investigation into environmental conditions.

Based on the above findings, we employed PeQD -CSSS as a NIR light source for the Yb unknown multiplexed gas detection, investigating technological approaches for analyzing the gas compositions (Fig. 6a-b). Fig. 6c shows the experimental optical setup, where gas molecules are positioned at the front of the spectrometer to provide absorption fingerprints about the gases. As depicted in Fig. 6d, the detection results encompass the typical marker gases such as hydrogen sulfide, ethylene, ammonia gas, ethanol, formaldehyde, and toluene. The highlighted circle markers indicate deviations in the NIR emission spectra of PeQD -CSSS attributable to gas Yb molecule absorption48. Notably, absorption peaks are observed at 1575, 1517, 973 and 1418 nm for hydrogen sulfide, ethylene, toluene and formaldehyde, respectively. The ethanol gas exhibits characteristic detection peaks at 1184 and 1459 nm. For ammonia gas, distinct peaks appear at 1165, 1531, 1544 and 2000 nm, offering enhanced detection specificity. This gas sensing system overcomes the drawbacks of poor selectivity for the gas sensors, such as semiconductor and electrochemical sensors, by allowing the simultaneous detection of several gas mixes since the emission spectra of PeQD -CSSS covers a wide NIR range (Supplementary Fig. 28). In these equations, y signifies the percentage relative reduction in the NIR spectral integral intensity and x denotes the gas concentration. The results of the testing and fitting curves are presented in Fig. 6e. This demonstrates that effective gas detection can be accomplished by harnessing the extensive NIR spectrum of PeQD -CSSS. The detection limits of the developed Yb NIR gas detection system for all six tested gases were calculated. The results indicated that all detection limits were below 20.7 ppm (Supplementary Table 3 and Note 2).

Furthermore, machine learning (ML)-assisted mixed gas detection at different concentrations from 100 to 700 ppm were conducted for better identification and monitoring of different gases (Supplementary Table 4, Note 3 and Supplementary Fig. 35). Random forest is a type of supervised learning algorithm that constructs multiple decision trees by randomly selecting samples and features, and achieves more accurate classification or regression results by integrating the predictions of these decision trees (Fig. 6f)4 9. The feature variables consist of “gas spectral lines” and “measurement results” in our work. Among them, “gas spectral lines” refer to the characteristic wavelength positions. “Measurement results” are the relative changes in the number of emitted photons within the absorption band of the target gas before and after gas introduction, calculated from the integral area of the spectrum. Together, these two types of features serve as the model independent variables, providing discriminative information from intrinsic gas properties and gas–spectrum interaction intensity. The prediction results are presented in Fig. 6g, demonstrating that gas detection with our NIR spectroscopy is highly effective in accurately distinguishing the components and concentration of gas mixtures, achieving 98.4% accuracy on the independent test set. This is further corroborated by the linear regression analysis of the mixed gas concentration shown in Fig. 6h. The fitted curve exhibits R2 of 0.996, indicating a high degree of consistency between the predicted and actual gas concentrations. Furthermore, when compared with the baseline models and other AI-based gas sensing studies in the IR domain, our approach exhibits notably superior accuracy performance for mixed gas detection (Supplementary Table 5 and 6). These findings fully demonstrate the significant potential of ML-assisted NIR spectroscopy induced by PeQD -CSSS heterostructure nanoparticles in accurately distinguishing the Yb composition and concentration of gas mixtures. To validate the high applicability of PeQD -CSSS Yb heterostructure nanoparticles in gas detection, we designed experiments to simulate the gas compositions of Planet 1, Planet 2, Planet 3, Planet 4, and Planet 5. The simulated gas compositions and their corresponding concentrations are presented in Supplementary Fig. 36. The test results, shown in Fig. 6i, demonstrate the accurate detection of gas types and concentrations for each simulated planetary environment. This approach offers a promising approach for exploring the atmospheric conditions and potential hazards of unknown environments in the future.

Gas Detection Process
The flow diagram of the gas detection system is illustrated in Fig. 6c. During spectral testing, the gas sample is introduced into a simple gas channel positioned between the NIR-emitting sample and the spectral acquisition detector. This configuration ensures full interaction between the gas and the incident infrared light, allowing the gas to absorb photons at its characteristic wavelengths. Consequently, the collected spectrum exhibits attenuation at these specific wavelengths, which serves as the basis for gas detection and quantification. The type of target gas can be determined based on its characteristic attenuation wavelength, while the gas concentration can be quantified by analyzing the intensity attenuation percentage at this wavelength. Together, these measurements enable a complete gas detection process. Throughout the procedure, a 365 nm ultraviolet laser was used as the excitation source, operating at a power density of 50 mW·cm-2.

In the measurements of luminescent dynamics, the samples were pumped using the Tektronix AFG1022 with a pulse duration of 10 ns, and a repetition frequency of 100 Hz. PLQY measurements were conducted on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS-1000 fluorescence spectrometer. The system was configured with an SM4 integrating sphere for light collection and employed a 150 W continuous-wave xenon lamp as the excitation source. The test samples were prepared by dispersion in cyclohexane, and the baseline was established using a blank reference cuvette filled with an equivalent volume of pure cyclohexane. This methodology ensures accurate photon counting for PLQY calculation by accounting for solvent scattering and absorption. Fianium WhiteLASE was employed as a white light excitation source in conjunction with a long-pass filter featuring a cutoff wavelength of 800 nm. The gas cylinders holding various target gases are connected to DGL-III gas and liquid distribution system (ELITE TECH). The system is capable of achieving high-precision control of the gas flow rate to obtain testing gases of different components and concentrations. Subsequently, the gases from this system are carried to the chamber for the measurement.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors proposed a novel sensitization mechanism (perovskite host→Yb3+ (perovskite) →Yb3+ (NaYF4) →Ln3+) in a perovskite@NaYF4 core-shell nanoparticles. This innovative approach addresses two critical challenges simultaneously: it overcomes the inherently small absorption cross-section of lanthanide ions while maintaining sufficient doping capacity. Particularly noteworthy is the mechanism's ability to achieve efficient broadband near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence emission under low-power white light excitation, a rare and significant advancement in the field. Furthermore, the authors employed this NIR light source to achieve precise classification of gas mixtures and simulate extraterrestrial gas exploration—an approach that holds significant scientific relevance. This multi-wavelength NIR luminescent composite structure holds significant potential for applications in diverse fields, including quantum communication and photonic chip development. Given its scientific merit and broad relevance, the manuscript appears suitable for publication in Nature Communications. However, I have several minor questions that I would like to address with the authors.
1. The excitation spectrum in Fig. 3a appears to be limited to approximately 660 nm. Could the authors clarify whether this range is constrained by the instrumentation's light source? Additionally, it would be valuable to understand if the material exhibits excitation responses at longer wavelengths. Please also specify the characteristic emission wavelengths corresponding to this excitation spectrum.
2. Figure 3f presents the emission spectrum under low-power white light excitation. For better characterization of the material's photophysical properties, could the authors please provide the power density of the excitation source used in these measurements? This quantitative information would significantly enhance the reproducibility and comparative analysis of the results.
3. Currently, non-toxic lanthanide-based halides (e.g., Cs2NaLnX6 and Cs3LnCl6) have attracted considerable research attention in this field. Could the composite structure proposed in this manuscript potentially employ these lanthanide-based halides as sensitizers, which would significantly mitigate material biotoxicity while maintaining comparable performance?
4. Could the authors include in the Supporting Information the experimental conditions used for spherical aberration-corrected electron microscopy in Figure 2? This would enhance the reproducibility of the work and provide valuable technical details for readers.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
General considerations
The authors presented a very detailed and scientifically sound investigation for the development of core-shell nanoparticles perfectly engineered to guarantee a broadband absorption in the visible range, together with a broad near-infrared photoluminescence emission. The limitations of some previous approaches from the literature were clearly discussed, and a novel technical solution was developed. Moreover, the material’s composition was optimized and tested on a specific application: the detection of gas molecules. The use of AI was also employed to verify the simultaneous identification and monitoring of multiple marker gases relevant to extraterrestrial exploration.
Strengths
My overall opinion on this research is very positive. The authors overcame several critical points, which were addressed by a well-planned scientific approach. They were able to understand the Physics beneath the energy transfer process and to optimize the materials composition to maximize absorption and emission. The idea of separating the absorption part from the emission part was excellent. Absorption was mediated by a PeQD, highly absorbing in the visible, while emission was obtained by a rare-earth-doped (RE3+) NaYF4 matrix, a well-known low phonon material with high RE3+ solubility.
An example of application for multiplexing gas sensing was also proposed and tested, considering several gases and compositions and obtaining a clear validation of the approach by the support of artificial intelligence.
Weaknesses
A key point for optical phosphors is the total quantum yield (QY = emitted photons / absorbed photons). The QY of the optimized nanoparticles should be reported and compared with other systems. Could the increased absorbance allow to overcome possible QY limitations in practical applications?
My main concern is about the proposed field of application: to be used, this technology needs to be brought in the place of analysis. This is highly limiting or impossible for planets far from Earth. Additionally, the possibility of sending other common equipment would probably be a preferred choice. This aspect requires better justification.
Finally, what is the detection limit for the different gases? Is it comparable to other approaches?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Y. Wang and co-workers report a novel hybrid material based on Yb3+-doped perovskite quantum dots (PeQDs) and Ln3+-doped NaYF4, leveraging the NIR emission of the Ln3+, while using the PeQDs as a novel antenna for efficient UV excitation. The optical data indicate strong enhancement of the NIR emission from the Ln-doped PeQD/NaYF4 core/shell/shell hybrids compared to pure Ln-doped NaYF4. This is potentially very interesting, with potential impact on the field. However, the paper does not provide the necessary experimental information and data to fully support the claims made. The authors stay vague when it comes to experimental details, and there is a lack of in-depth characterization. Some claims are not supported by the findings. Therefore, I cannot recommend publication of the manuscript.
Detailed comments are provided in the following.
1. The authors claim that the underlaying mechanism is a quantum cutting process. However, there are no data provided to confirm that. In-depth analysis of the quantum yield (QY) would be required, unveiling QY values of close to 200% (or at least larger than 100%). Conversely, the authors only briefly mention a QY value of 23%. No details are provided how this value was obtained.
2. The Experimental Details section is very poor, lacking information. It would not be possible to repeat the described experiments. For instance:
a. Dopant concentrations in mol% and their respective amounts (mg, mol) should be added.
b. There is no procedure provided that explains the growth of the NaYF4 shells on the PeQDs. The section Synthesis of QDYb@NaYF4: Ln3+@NaYF4 (Ln=Yb, Ho, Er, Tm, Ce) NCs does not mention how the QDs are introduced into the reaction.
c. Figure 1: CSSS NC? This NP architecture is not described in the Experimental details.
d. Why was a Nd laser (and the third harmonic) used for excitation? Why not a simple UV excitation source? This would be particularly relevant to demonstrate the possible use of low-P excitation.
e. Excitation power density information is missing.
f. It is not clear whether the PL data are obtained in solid state or on dispersions (Concentration of NPs in the dispersion? Solvent used?).
g. Experimental details about the gas sensing are not sufficient to allow for reproduction of the experiment.
3. Data provided in the ESI are poorly described in the figure captions and/or are not sufficient to support the claims made. For instance:
a. A too small number of NPs is shown in TEM images. Larger areas with more NPs need to be shown to confirm the homogeneity of the samples. TEM images and size distribution plots including average sizes and standard deviation should be provided for all core-only, core/shell, core/shell/shell, and core/shell/shell/shell NPs. Information about shell thickness should be provided for all shells in all samples.
b. Dopant concentration should be included in the figure captions.
c. EDX mapping: TEM images of the region of interest should be added; scale bars are missing. E.g. Fig S2: What are the data series in a, b, c, and d? “elemental line scan analysis curves” – what is meant by this caption?
d. All photoluminescence spectra should be labeled with f-f transitions.
e. All photoluminescence spectra should show numbers on the y-axis to allow for comparison of the intensities (ESI and main text). Without numbers, the claimed enhancement is not visible.
f. It is not clear what is meant by “NaYF4, monitoring wavelength of 1180nm.” (Fig S6 and elsewhere). Such wording indicates that the shown data are an excitation spectrum. On the other hand, excitation spectra shown in the manuscript and ESI lack information about the monitored wavelength.
g. XPS spectra should be labeled (and deconvoluted is necessary).
h. Information about I, Br, Cl amounts is missing in Figures S12 and S13 (meaning of the shades of green and rainbow, respectively).
i. Figure S15: It is not clear what the y-axis means. The z-axis should show values to allow for the comparison of the emission intensities obtained for the different compositions.
j. Information about excitation wavelength, laser power density, and solvent and NP concentration in the dispersion (or solid state?) are missing.
4. Confirmation that the set concentration for Ce in mol% was indeed incorporated should be provided (e.g., ICP).
5. Confirmation of the PeQD/NaYF4 structure (Figure 2): Elemental mapping of the core elements is missing. EDX in Fig 2d is not convincing for the QD elements. Could error bars be added to Figure 2f to demonstrate homogeneity of the samples. Fig 2f: Which element does the half-filled blue hexagon symbol represent?
6. Power-dependent spectra should be shown to support statements about the power threshold.
7. “Furthermore, we combine 257 CsPbCl1.5Br1.5: Yb3+ PeQDs with CSSS…” – how was this done? What is the resulting structure?
8. Fig 4a: it is not clear from which spectral range is cut from the x-axis by the axis cut (and why it is cut).
9. What are the 4 bars per mechanism in Fig 4d? What is x in the legend?
10. Gas sensing: What is the LOD for the gas sensor? A comparison of the sensing performance with established sensors and other sensors reported in the literature should be provided.
Additional comments:
- English language needs major revision. Some sentences are difficult to follow (especially in the experimental details section). For instance (there are many more errors or unclear wording):
o What is meant by „highly doped Ln3+ ions within“ (a host can be highly doped but not an ion)?
o All the processes must be refilled with N2. – It is not clear what this means.
o It was continued heated at 160 °C for 1 h and refilled with N2. Then the solution was then increased to 240 °C and maintained for 20 minutes. Then Cs-oleate (0.8 mL) was quickly injected into the bottle… - It is not clear what this means.
o The anion source after complete solubilization…
o XRD curves
o Notably, our distinctive technical involves…
o Further to incorporate Yb3+ ion in the outer NaYF4 shell, the spectral obtained from the PeQD@NaYF4: Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ …
o Yb3+ lifetime decay - either lifetime or decay
- Figure 4b and c: The x-axis label is not correct - should be time, not lifetime.
- The authors introduce Ln3+ ions as lanthanum ions. This is not correct. Lanthanum has the elemental symbol La, and La3+ ions do not undergo any f-f transitions, hence, no luminescence.
- Introduction: Examples given for NIR emitting Ln-based phosphors is very limited. It is not clear how they were chosen. Additional context and description of state-of-the-art NIR Ln-based emitters should be included. Likewise, the Introduction lacks discussion of the state-of- the-art of NIR-based gas sensors.
- The abbreviation for the system and the energy pathway introduced at line 86, page 4, is difficult to understand.
- The authors claim that high energy lasers are a drawback of conventional Ln-based phosphors. Direct Ln excitation does not require high-energy lasers. Such statement is mis-leading (and incorrect).
- Building on the previous study,… - a reference should be provided.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The scope of this review is only on the machine learning (ML) aspects of the gas sensing reported in the manuscript.
The manuscript presents the application of a ML method, namely random forest (RF), in utilizing the extensive near infrared spectrum of Cl1.5Br1.5-PeQDYb@CSSS, to predict labels and concentrations of several gas molecules (ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, ethanol, ethene, toluene, and formaldehyde).
My overall recommendation is to accept with major revisions only on the ML aspect of the gas sensing reported in the manuscript. Please note my recommendations do not go beyond the machine learning (ML) aspects of the gas sensing reported in the manuscript.
The paragraph (lines 403-425) describing the ML aspects is too short and lacks key details regarding the methodology and its soundness for the AI-driven gas sensing analysis.
Specifically, the following points should be addressed, and relevant details should be provided.
1. Please clarify the training-testing splits or folds. Please also provide the total number of samples in the train and test set as well. Without that contextual information the accuracy metric of 98.4% is difficult to assess. Since for larger train split and smaller test split the accuracy metric may simply reflect repeatability. Furthermore, was the metric calculated based on a k-fold cross-validation average? Please also specify the number of trees used, tree depth, splitting criteria, class weighting, hyper parameter search strategy, and the cross validation scheme (k fold? Leave-one-out? stratified?) as well.
2. In lines 408-409, it is stated that “characteristic wavelength and peak intensity change” are utilized for speciation and quantification, however Fig. 5b–c suggests the full spectrum is available for the model to learn. Was the RF model built on raw intensities, hand‑picked peaks, or engineered features? Was the model fed with individual signals or signals converted to images? A schematic (similar to Fig. 5d) and complete feature (independent variables) list would help clarify the inputs and outputs to the RF model greatly benefit the sensor community in pursuing AI-sensor integration for gas-phase species detection in the future.
3. Narayanan and Kappor stated in a recently published comment (Nature 640, 312-314 (2025) doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-025-01067-2),
“Our concern is mainly about these modelling-based approaches, in which AI is used to make predictions or test hypotheses about how a system functions. One common source of error is ‘leakage’, an issue that arises when information from a model’s evaluation data improperly influences its training process. When this happens, a machine-learning model might simply memorize patterns in the evaluation data instead of capturing the meaningful patterns behind the phenomenon of interest. This limits the real-world applicability of such models and produces little in terms of scientific knowledge.”
With that context and the effects of leakage in mind, ensemble models, such as RF, requires fine tuning or pruning techniques to work well. The authors should state and briefly discuss if such techniques were implemented to address the issues of overfitting and leakage?
4. The manuscript lacks benchmarks against recent AI based gas sensing studies in the IR domain, where these same molecules have been classified and quantified in both pure and mixed samples, using several deep learning models as well as classical ML models and ensemble models, from experiments as well as simulated data. I recommend including at least one baseline model for speciation and concentration prediction comparison for each molecule, and report uncertainty (e.g., confidence intervals, fold wise SDs, or precision–recall curves) to strengthen methodological rigor. Because this work’s main departures from prior studies are the simulated planetary conditions and the new sensor platform, providing those comparisons will let readers determine the true performance gains.
5. In Figure 5d, the numbering of the decision trees in the random forest model appears to be incorrect. Each tree is numbered as 1.
6. Recent work has shown AI assisted gas sensing for both trace and mixed gas environments. This manuscript’s strength lies in its quantum engineered nanocrystals, yet lines 33 34 of the abstract imply a broader advance in AI sensor integration. The AI/ML section is too brief to assess such novelty since only simulated mixtures in assumed planetary environments, pressure/temperature variations, are provided, and the results Fig. 5g is a proof of concept simulation. This should be clearly stated so as not to expand the claim presented in this study.

The reviewer #3:
Thank you for the valuable comments on our work. Below are the replies to your review comments.
Comment 1: That the authors claim that the underlaying mechanism is a quantum cutting process. However, there are no data provided to confirm that. In-depth analysis of the quantum yield (QY) would be required, unveiling QY values of close to 200% (or at least larger than 100%). Conversely, the authors only briefly mention a QY value of 23%. No details are provided how this value was obtained.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comments. This study employs CsPbCl Br : 1.5 1.5 Yb3+ as the core of the composite material. This quantum cutting material has been widely recognized in the literature as a highly efficient luminescent system, exhibiting a remarkable photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) approaching 200% (Adv. Mater., 2017, 13,1704149; Nano Lett., 2019, 19, 6904-6913; Energy Environ. Sci., 2019, 12, 2486; Nano Lett., 2019, 19, 338-341). To ensure the reliability of our measurements, we conducted multiple independent verifications of the core material's PLQY throughout the experimental process. The corresponding PLQY result is 148.35% (presented in Figure a), representing a typical quantum cutting process.
Building upon this foundation, we have successfully implemented a directed energy transfer process that utilizes the efficient quantum cutting emission of Yb3+ ions and their collaborative energy transfer to generate rare-earth ion infrared emission. The 23% PLQY value corresponds to the PLQY of the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+@NaYF :Er3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Yb3+, Ce3+@NaYF nanocrystals, measured at an emission of 1527 nm under 365 nm 4 excitation. This PLQY value is lower than the quantum cutting result as the energy transfer from the quantum cutting core (CsPbCl Br : Yb3+) to shell (NaYF :Er3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Yb3+, Ce3+) lead to partial photon losses. Furthermore, during the revision of the manuscript, the PLQY of the NIR (900-1700 nm) emission from CsPbCl Br : 1.5 1.5 Yb3+@CSSS nanocrystals was evaluated under 365 nm excitation and was determined to be approximately 37.1%. The PLQY was measured using an Edinburgh Instruments FLS1000 spectrometer equipped with an integrating sphere. The sample, prepared as a diluted low-concentration solution, exhibited a PLQY. The description of the PLQY in the main text has been revised accordingly (page 13, lines 3–7 and 17-18). Please refer to the updated version for review.
Figure a. PLQY of the CsPbCl Br : Yb core material. A quantum yield of 148.35% 1.5 1.5 under 365 nm excitation provides experimental validation of the quantum cutting mechanism.

After training and parameter optimization, the prediction accuracy of the model on the test set data that was not involved in the training can objectively reflect the actual generalization performance of the model. For the model optimization, the grid search strategy was employed for hyperparameter search. The optimal parameter combination was screened by iterating through the key parameter grid of the random forest and combining with 5-fold stratified cross-validation. The "stratified" design ensures that the class distribution of data in each fold during cross-validation is consistent with that of the original dataset, effectively avoiding evaluation bias caused by data distribution imbalance and thus guaranteeing the objectivity of the model generalization ability evaluation.

Firstly, Fig. 5b depicts the relative change in the number of emitted photons within the absorption band before and after introducing the target gas. The primary purpose is to verify the discriminative value of the characteristic wavelengths for gas species identification of our designed new light source from a physical perspective. Fig. 5c illustrates the spectral attenuation trend as a function of concentration for a single target gas, explaining the scientific rationale for quantifying concentration based on changes in emitted photons. These two figures focus on extracting the physical significance of key features, aiming to justify the design of the model inputs rather than directly presenting the full spectral input dimensions of the model. We emphasize this distinction to avoid any potential misunderstanding.
Secondly, the model inputs are neither raw spectral intensities nor simply manually selected peaks. Instead, the feature variables consist of “gas spectral lines” and “measurement results.” “Gas spectral lines” refer to the characteristic wavelength positions automatically output by the spectrometer through spectral analysis. “Measurement results” are the relative changes in the number of emitted photons within the absorption band of the target gas before and after gas introduction, calculated from the integral area of the spectrum. Together, these two types of features serve as the model independent variables, providing discriminative information from two dimensions: “intrinsic gas properties” and “gas–spectrum interaction intensity.”
The model inputs are provided as structured numerical feature vectors rather than converted into image signals. This ensures the model focuses on key discriminative information and avoids the impact of redundant full-spectrum data on training efficiency.

Comment 3: Narayanan and Kappor stated in a recently published comment (Nature 640, 312-314 (2025) doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-025-01067-2), “Our concern is mainly about these modelling-based approaches, in which AI is used to make predictions or test hypotheses about how a system functions. One common source of error is ‘leakage’, an issue that arises when information from a model’s evaluation data improperly influences its training process. When this happens, a machine-learning model might simply memorize patterns in the evaluation data instead of capturing the meaningful patterns behind the phenomenon of interest. This limits the real-world applicability of such models and produces little in terms of scientific knowledge.” With that context and the effects of leakage in mind, ensemble models, such as RF, requires fine tuning or pruning techniques to work well. The authors should state and briefly discuss if such techniques were implemented to address the issues of overfitting and leakage?
Response: Thank you for your valuable comments. We highly agree with the concerns raised by Narayan and Kapoor regarding "data leakage" and model generalization in their literature, which is also a core issue that our study has focused on preventing and controlling in model design and data processing.
To prevent overfitting risks, a combined strategy of "parameter grid search + model complexity constraint" is adopted to achieve effective prevention. This essentially equates to the "fine-tuning and pruning optimization" of the integrated model. Through GridSearchCV combined with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, multi-dimensional parameter grids are designed for the classification and regression tasks to fine-tune core parameters such as n_estimators and max_depth. Among them, the optimization of max_depth can directly control the complexity of a single decision tree to avoid overfitting caused by excessive tree depth, which is equivalent to the "pruning" operation of the base learners in the integrated model. The optimization of n_estimators balances the model variance and bias, ensuring a balance between "fitting sufficiency" and "generalization stability". For the classification task, "stratified sampling" is used to divide the training/test sets in an 8:2 ratio to ensure the consistency of sample distribution.
In terms of data leakage prevention, StandardScaler is used to standardize the input features to eliminate differences in scale. All operations involving random processes are fixed with random_state = 42. This setting not only ensures that the sample division results and the initial state of the model in different experiments are completely consistent to achieve result reproducibility, but also fundamentally avoids the implicit data leakage risk introduced by the uncertainty of the random process.
We have provided the relevant descriptions of model in “Database and method in Supplementary Note 2” part in in Supporting Information.

(c) The schematics in Fig 2a and 2f are not in agreement with the data shown in Fig.2: The schematics show core/shell/shell architecture. The data were obtained on core/shell (based on the figure caption). Also, with respect to the discussion of that figure at Page 10, line 242: The addition of an outer undoped shell is described. Subsequently, the description of data shown in Fig 2 seem to revolve around samples prior such addition of the undoped shell. This is confusing.
Response (c):
We acknowledge the reviewer's attention to detail regarding the XPS sample. The data presented in Figure 2 (including XPS, TEM, and optical characterizations) were acquired from the intermediate CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ 1.5 1.5 4 heterostructure (without the outer undoped NaYF shell). This decision was based 4 on two key reasons: first, the outermost undoped NaYF passivation shell (≈4 nm) 4 would significantly obscure the spatial distribution of PeQDs and Er/Yb/Ce in electron microscopy characterizations (e.g., EDS mapping resolution would be compromised, making it impossible to distinguish Er signals from the NaYF :Yb3+, 4 Ln3+ functional shell vs. background). Comparative TEM images (Figure R3) demonstrate that the intermediate structure avoids this shielding effect, enabling clear visualization of the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ interface and 1.5 1.5 4 element distribution. Second, this approach ensures analytical consistency across all techniques. Characterizing the intermediate structure is sufficient to verify the core objective—successful formation of the CsPbX : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, 3 4 Ln3+@NaYF NPs. The outermost passivation shell is a subsequent optimization 4 step (for stability/luminescence efficiency) that does not alter the elemental distribution or interface properties.
The original schematics in Figure 2a and 2f were intended to illustrate the complete synthetic route of our final optimized sample (CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Er3+, Ce3+@NaYF ), but we failed to clearly distinguish it from the actual tested 4 sample (CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+) in the initial version. 1.5 1.5 4 We have updated the schematics in Figure 2a and 2f to accurately represent the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ structure of the samples used for the 1.5 1.5 4 tests in Figure 2. On Page 9, Line 22-26, we have clarified the timeline of sample preparation and testing: “Since the inert NaYF coating can obscure the resolution 4 of the PeQD, characterization was performed on uncoated CsPbCl Br : Yb3+- 1.5 1.5 NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ NPs (Figure S11-12). The addition of an outer undoped 4 NaYF shell was a subsequent optimization step to enhance material stability and 4 luminescence efficiency. The data presented in Figure 2 were obtained from the intermediate heterostructure samples prior to this outer shell modification, aiming to validate the successful formation of the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Ce3+ heterostructure.”
Figure R3. TEM morphology comparison between PeQD -NaYF : Er, Yb, Ce@ Yb 4 NaYF and PeQD -NaYF : Er, Yb, Ce.
(d) Scheme in Fig 4f is miss-leading as it depicts a clear core/shell boarder between PeQDs and NaYF4:Ln (based on discussion and data, the PeQDs rather seem to be embedded into a NaYF4:Ln matrix.
Response (d):
Thank you for your perceptive observation and valuable feedback. To clarify, the actual structure of the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ component is 1.5 1.5 4 multiple discrete CsPbCl Br : Yb3+ PeQDs uniformly dispersed and embedded 1.5 1.5 within a continuous NaYF :Ln matrix, rather than a separate core-shell 4 configuration with a clear interface. Response (e):
Thank you for your perceptive observation and valuable feedback. To clearly demonstrate the formation of the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ 1.5 1.5 4 heterostructure, we deliberately used the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Ce3+ intermediate structure (rather than the final CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Er3+, Ce3+@ NaYF architecture) for the characterization in Figure 2 (including 4 TEM, HRTEM, line scanning, EDS mapping, and XPS) as was explained in Response (c).
The EDS mapping and line scanning data in Figure 2f clearly confirm that Er is concentrated in the NaYF :Er,Yb,Ce layer for CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, 4 1.5 1.5 4 Er3+, Ce3+ heterostructure, which also indicated that the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+ PeQDs 1.5 1.5 were successfully ensembled in NaYF :Ln matrix. The original contradiction arose 4 from failing to state the measured sample is CsPbCl Br : Yb3+-NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, 1.5 1.5 4 Ce3+ heterostructure.
The updated Figure 2a has placed particular emphasis on the measured sample (CsPbCl Br :Yb-NaYF₄: Er,Yb,Ce heterostructure). Please refer to the updated 1.5 1.5 Figure 2.
(f) In addition, it is not clear how multiple PeQDs can fit within the given core matrix. For instance, Fig S23: The PeQDs are shown to be ca. 11 nm in size. After first “shelling”, the size is 21 nm. How many PeQDs are embedded in the NaYF4:Ln matrix? What is the size of the PeQDs after possible shelling-induced dissolution?

Response (f):
Thank you for your valuable suggestions. The spatial resolution of EDS mapping is compromised in the CsPbCl Br : Yb3+- 1.5 1.5 NaYF : Yb3+, Er3+, Ce3+ structure due to the extremely small inter-particle spacing 4 and high density of the PeQDs. Under these conditions, the electron beam interaction volume and secondary fluorescence effects generate extensive false signals and artifacts. Comment 2: Experimental details still lack information required to reproduce the experiments. For instance:
“Then 0.8 mL of cesium oleate solution was rapidly injected.” - What is the concentration of the Cs oleate solution? Providing the volume alone will not allow the reader to reproduce the synthesis.

The updated sentence is: "Then, 0.8 mL of the pre-prepared Cs-oleate solution (0.09 mol/L) was rapidly injected."
The term "5 mL of the pre-synthesized NPs supernatant" in the synthesis step refers to the supernatant collected after the NPs were redispersed in 5 mL of cyclohexane, subjected to ultrasonic dispersion, and allowed to settle. This value has been added to the Supporting Information (page 4, line 1) and is marked in yellow for your review. To guarantee batch-to-batch comparability, all syntheses are conducted under rigorously identical conditions.
PLQY measurements were conducted on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS-1000 fluorescence spectrometer. The system was configured with an SM4 integrating sphere for light collection and employed a 150 W continuous-wave xenon lamp as the excitation source. The test samples were prepared by dispersion in cyclohexane, and the baseline was established using a blank reference cuvette filled with an equivalent volume of pure cyclohexane. This methodology ensures accurate photon counting for PLQY calculation by accounting for solvent scattering and absorption. A comprehensive description of this procedure can be found on Page 8 of the Supplementary Information, with the relevant text highlighted for easy identification.
Comment 3: Quantum cutting is represented in Scheme 1 (right) as taking place for the PeQD host to Yb energy transfer. If that was the case, a more than 100% QY would be expected for the Yb3+ emission in a control sample that consists of PeQDs:Yb. The author mention this in their response letter and Figure a therein. This data and discussion should be provided in the manuscript (or SI).
Response：
Thank you for your insightful feedback. As recommended, we have added a discussion on the Yb-doped PeQDs that exhibit a PLQY exceeding 100% to the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Note 1 in page 9), and provide clear explain in the yellow-highlighted section on page 6 of the manuscript. The added text has been highlighted for your convenience.
Comment 4: Size distribution histograms and HRTEM images
Counts axis in all size distribution plots should include values to indicate how many NPs were subjected to size analysis (Fig S1 and elsewhere).
The size distribution for the PeQDs in Fig S23 seems to have a too small standard deviation. Looking at the obvious size variations in the TEM image and the broadness of the histogram (from 8 to 15 nm), a standard deviation of 0.17 nm seems not to be realistic. Is this indeed the standard deviation or rather the error of the fit? Same for the other histograms in Fig. S23 (and elsewhere across the manuscript / SI): standard deviations seem to be too small for the histograms given.
Scale bars are missing in the HRTEM plots in Fig S1 and elsewhere.
Response: Thank you for your keen observation and valuable suggestions. The error value in the previous size distribution histogram represented the Gaussian fitting deviation. We apologize for any confusion this may have caused. The graph has now been updated to indicate the actual size deviation, and following your suggestion, the vertical axis has been revised to display the number of nanoparticles measured. Furthermore, scale bars have been added to the HRTEM images. We welcome your review of these revisions.
Comment 5: XRD reference patterns
Reference numbers for XRD patterns are provided in Fig S2 and S16 but the chemical composition and phase of these references are missing.
Fig S10 mentions a reference card but not reference data are added to the plot.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. The sample characterized in Figure S2 and S16 has the composition NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+@NaYF (Ln = Ho, Er, Tm, Ce) and 4 4 PeQD -NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+@NaYF (Ln=Ho, Er, Tm, Ce) heterostructure, respectively. Yb 4 4 Due to the length of the formula, an abbreviation is used in the figure for clarity. The full chemical details are provided in the accompanying notes. The samples in Figure S2 all exhibit a hexagonal crystal structure. Please also note that the heterostructure in Figure S16 is composed of cubic-phase CsPbCl Br : Yb3+ and hexagonal-phase 1.5 1.5 NaYF : Yb3+, Ln3+@NaYF (Ln=Ho, Er, Tm, Ce). These details are now provided in 4 4 the updated annotations.
Furthermore, we have included the standard reference card in Figure S10, as shown below (Figure R4). Please see the revised manuscript.
Figure R4 (Figure S10). X-ray powder diffraction patterns (XRD) for CSSS (NaYF : 4 6% Ho3+, 20% Yb3+, 6% Ce3+@NaYF : 5% Er3+, 35% Yb3+, 4% Ce3+@NaYF : 0.6% 4 4 Tm3+, 25% Yb3+@ NaYF ). 4
Comment 6: Wording in Abstract
It is suggested to tone down the wording in the abstract:
What is meant by quantum-engineering?
“unprecedented absorption bandwidth (200–690 nm) across the UV-visible spectrum, 27 enabling efficient excitation at sub-microwatt levels (50 μW cm-2).”: At 50uW cm-2, the emission cannot be called efficient. It is barely visible in the provided PL spectrum. Indeed, most spectra shown were obtained at power densities that are orders of magnitudes higher, including the gas sensing. At what power density were the reported QY values obtained? This statement in the abstract is miss-leading.
Response:
Thank you for this insightful feedback. In this study, "quantum-engineering" denotes the mechanism we proposed that facilitates efficient energy transfer within the heterostructure via a quantum cutting process. To prevent any potential confusion, we have replaced the term with "quantum cutting-engineering" for greater precision. The revision is highlighted on page 2, line 7 of the revised manuscript.
We agree with the comment that the emission at 50 µW cm-2 could not be described as efficient and have therefore revised the abstract accordingly. The updated text now states: "The designed heterostructure exhibits an unprecedented absorption bandwidth (200–690 nm) across the UV-visible spectrum, with an exceptionally low stimulation threshold at the sub-microwatt level (50 µW cm-2)." This revision can be found in the abstract on page 2, lines 9–11.
As noted in our response to Question 2, the PLQY was measured under a 365 nm power density of ~200 mW cm-2. This differs from the lower power spectral tests due to the use of different, specialized instruments. The PLQY system's light source operates at this fixed power. Crucially, the linear nature of the luminescence ensures that the reported PLQY is independent of this excitation power.
Comment 7: Referencing
The introduction should not ignore previous work on Ln-NPs that demonstrated Tm and Ho emission at 1400 and 2000 nm, respectively.
Response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We agree that prior studies on Ln-doped nanoparticles (Ln-NPs) featuring emissions at ~1400 nm and ~2000 nm are important to contextualize our work. Accordingly, in the Introduction (page 3, line 21), we have integrated a discussion on the ~1460 nm emission of Tm³⁺ and the ~2000 nm emission of Ho³⁺, supported by appropriate citations, to provide a more comprehensive research background. These additions are now available for your review.
